newsitem.title: USA: Groups push to spend designated funds on US parks.
newsitem.headline: Groups push to spend designated funds on US parks.

text.p: Americans were being deprived of parks and wilderness areas because lawmakers for years have hoarded billions of dollars intended for purchasing public lands, environmentalist groups said Friday.
A coalition of groups said it would campaign to pressure Congress and the Clinton administration to use the Land and Water Conservation Fund to buy lands instead of defraying federal budget deficit.

"It's an absolute travesty that the money is not being used for the purposes for which it was originally intended," Donald Murphy, director of California state parks and a coalition member, said at a news conference.

Congress set up the fund with the idea that a share of royalties paid to the government by companies for extracting oil and natural gas from offshore drilling should be used to replenish natural resources elsewhere. Since 1980, $8 billion has been used for the fund's stated purpose of buying and improving public lands and giving states and local governments matching grants for recreation programmes.

But another $11 billion has been used for other purposes -- largely to reduce the deficit -- which is legal because the conservation fund is not a true trust fund. But the coalition said lawmakers were breaking a deal that environmental risks of offshore drilling be offset by improvements on land.

The fund's share of royalties raises $900 million annually. In the last two years, $139 million and $150 million actually went to the public lands fund, while the rest went to the budget's general fund.

Murphy said the coalition expected to raise $1 million by June and will conduct an advertising campaign "with the ultimate goal to commit Congress to fully funding the Land and Water Conservation Fund."

The coalition, called Americans for Our Heritage and Recreation, represents interests including parks and recreation specialists, conservationsists, the outdoor recreation goods industry, civic groups and others.
Senate Energy Committee Chairman Frank Murkowski also said he would push to free more of the land funds.

"Why should we allow $10 billion to languish in federal coffers masking the size of the deficit?" the Alaska Republican asked in a statement. He said he will try to reinstate the portion of the fund used for state grants, about $25 million annually, which was cut off two years ago.

But Senate Appropriations Committee spokesman John Raffeto said parks and public lands were among many competing interests seeking federal dollars. "Everybody's pulling at the purse strings and the Appropriations Committee is facing this problem" of growth in entitlement programmes and demand for other spending, he said.
